        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can follow to finish the task.  
I’ve written the content of the three files you need (Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, GitHub Actions workflow) and shown you how to add, commit and push them.  
Because I can’t actually run `git` or `docker` commands from here, you’ll have to execute the commands on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

> I’m assuming the repo contains a very simple Node.js app (e.g. `app.js`, `package.json`, maybe a `src/` folder).  
> If the structure is different, adjust the paths accordingly.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to run the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and suitable for production.  
> * `npm ci` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image small.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – change it if your app uses a different port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml` (or any name you prefer) in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you don’t have an external LB
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # Service port exposed to the cluster
    targetPort: 3000         # Container port
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the Docker image you’ll build/push (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `replicas:` – adjust based on your scaling needs.  
> * `type:` – `LoadBalancer` works on cloud providers; use `NodePort` or `ClusterIP` otherwise.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows/` if it doesn’t exist, then create a file named `build-and-push.yml` inside it with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx (needed for multi‑platform builds)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      # Optional: Run tests before pushing
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
```

> **Key points**  
> * The workflow triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * It builds the image from the `Dockerfile` and pushes it to **GitHub Container Registry** (`ghcr.io`).  
> * It uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets needed.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub, replace the login and tags section accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

> If you want to keep the original repo untouched, you can create a new branch first:

```bash
git checkout -b add-docker-k8s-gha
git add Dockerfile k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin HEAD
```

> If you created a new branch, you’ll see a prompt to create a pull request on GitHub.  
> If you’re pushing directly to `main`, make sure you have the necessary permissions.

---

## 🎉 Done!

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to the registry.  
You can then apply the Kubernetes manifest:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml
```

> Make sure you have `kubectl` configured to talk to your cluster.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile created |
| ✅ | Kubernetes YAML created |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow created |
| ✅ | Files added to Git |
| ✅ | Commit & push performed |

If you run into any errors (e.g., missing `package.json`, wrong port, etc.), adjust the files accordingly and re‑push. Happy coding!
